title: Mornings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Ypsilanti data center proposal highlights water, power stakes for Michigan towns.

lines.text: Good morning, and welcome to Mornings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
It's Monday, August 10, and we're kicking off with a look at how one Washtenaw County proposal is putting water and power tradeoffs front and center for communities across the state.
That Ypsilanti plan sounds like a perfect window into the bigger fight. Graham, what stood out from yesterday's coverage?
Eastern Echo reported on a presentation where EMU hydrogeologist Christopher Gellasch explained closed-loop cooling systems that can reuse groundwater without warming the subsurface.
Interesting. So the tech side says it can be managed?
That's what he laid out. Activist Peter Sinclair added that new energy infrastructure could actually benefit the community if it's done right.
But we're hearing a lot of pushback elsewhere. How does this fit into the statewide picture?
Exactly. This Ypsilanti discussion comes as multiple townships are drafting rules to limit size, noise, and power use before projects even apply.
Like the Lowell Township planning commission today?
Yes, and similar efforts in West Michigan and Detroit. Officials want to avoid the heavy electricity and water demands that have already sparked fights in other parts of the state.
What kind of history are we talking about here?
Data centers have been eyeing Michigan for years because of available land and power, but recent AI-driven proposals have accelerated everything.
And the stakes for regular residents?
Attorney General Dana Nessel is calling on the Public Service Commission to block utilities from shifting infrastructure costs to ratepayers.
That could mean higher monthly bills if those big deals go through unchecked.
Nessel made that clear in statements today and earlier this week, saying the commission must protect residents from hidden subsidies for big tech.
How much power are we talking about?
Proposals can add hundreds of megawatts, straining grids in places like Mason County and metro Detroit where utilities are already asking questions about upgrades.
And water?
Cooling is the big one. Even closed-loop systems raise concerns about long-term groundwater use and quality in rural and suburban areas.
Who are the main players pushing back locally?
Township planning commissions, state senators warning about rate hikes, and groups like the one Peter Sinclair is part of.
What about the companies?
Developers are pitching on-site power options to bypass grid delays, but that brings its own questions about emissions and noise.
And OpenAI stepped in on Friday with cybersecurity help after a water system hack.
Right, tied directly to utilities that would serve these new facilities.
So what's the risk for towns without strong rules?
They could end up subsidizing projects through higher utility bills or strained infrastructure, as a state senator flagged for suburbs around Detroit.
How far could the impacts reach?
Residents 30 miles away in other DTE or Consumers Energy territories might see rate effects if large loads aren't managed.
What happens next in Ypsilanti specifically?
The conversation is still early, but it shows how local experts and activists are trying to shape any future applications.
And across the state?
More townships are expected to follow Lowell and others with ordinances or moratorium proposals before projects land.
Any sense of timeline?
The Public Service Commission will likely face more pressure from Nessel's office in the coming weeks on those power deals.
And for farmland and small towns?
Zoning limits on size and noise are the main tools they're reaching for to protect those areas.
Does the Ypsilanti plan change the conversation?
It adds concrete details from a hydrogeologist on how cooling might work, which could inform other communities.
But Sinclair's point about potential benefits is also getting airtime.
Yes, new infrastructure as a possible upside if the grid upgrades are paid for by the developers.
How are utilities responding so far?
They're in the middle of it, with some already presenting demand forecasts to local boards.
What should listeners watch for this week?
The meetings today in Lowell and London Township will give the first public looks at proposed ordinances.
Any other angles on the water side?
The closed-loop discussion in Ypsilanti is new detail that could ease some concerns or raise others about long-term reuse.
And power deals?
Nessel's push to the PSC is the key statewide lever right now.
How does this compare to fights in other states?
Michigan is still earlier in the curve, which is why local rules are being written proactively.
What could tip the balance?
Whether the PSC adopts stronger oversight on cost allocation and whether more townships pass limits before applications arrive.
Any early signs of compromise?
The expert presentations like Gellasch's suggest developers and locals are at least starting to talk specifics.
Bottom line for ratepayers?
If deals get approved without protections, monthly bills could rise across service territories.
And for water resources?
Communities with good local zoning will have more say in how much is drawn and how it's managed.
What's your take on the momentum?
It's building fast, with today's meetings and Nessel's latest calls showing real movement.
Thanks for laying that out. Let's move to quick hits on the other stories.
Today Lowell Township is advancing a new ordinance on data center size, noise, and power.
And Nessel is pressing the PSC again on blocking cost shifts to regular customers.
Yesterday West Michigan officials got their first detailed look at how these projects could affect roads and electric demand.
A state senator also warned local leaders about rate and water risks in metro Detroit suburbs.
On Friday Mason County questioned whether the local grid can handle the surge.
Detroit released its own assessment showing hundreds of megawatts of new demand.
And a Michigan firm pitched on-site power generation to speed things up.
Plus the OpenAI offer on water utility cybersecurity after that hack.
Now for on deck, the meetings listeners can attend today.
London Township Board of Trustees is taking up a data center ordinance.
And Lowell Charter Township Planning Commission has both an ordinance and moratorium proposal on the agenda.
Check the Michigan Data Center Tracker for times and locations.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Ypsilanti Plan Puts Water and Power Tradeoffs in Spotlight
